title: MagiCache: A Virtual In-Cache Computing Engine
problem: Array-level in-cache computing architectures dedicate entire cache arrays as compute arrays, leaving most computing lines idle at runtime while the non-computing arrays absorb large bursty memory accesses—both causing severe on-chip capacity loss and high data movement latency for data-parallel applications.
motivation: Data-parallel workloads demand high parallelism and energy efficiency, and in-cache computation can eliminate cache-to-processor data movement, but existing coarse-grained array-level designs waste capacity because only a few rows per array are active at any time.
method: MagiCache allows each cache array to dynamically switch individual rows between being compute lines or regular cache lines on the fly, rather than dedicating entire arrays to one role. A virtual engine (software running on the chip) monitors what the program needs at each moment—how much storage versus how much computing—and reallocates rows accordingly. To handle sudden bursts of memory requests without stalling, MagiCache uses instruction chaining: it schedules compute operations and memory requests out-of-order and in parallel, so the long wait for data from HBM/DRAM (the main memory) overlaps with ongoing computation.
key_novelty: MagiCache dynamically reallocates individual cache rows between compute and storage roles and uses instruction chaining to hide memory latency, eliminating the fixed capacity loss of array-level in-cache architectures.
contributions: Cacheline-level in-cache computing architecture allowing per-row dynamic assignment as compute or cache with negligible overhead.
A virtual engine for runtime space management that allocates rows based on observed computation and storage demands.
Instruction chaining technique for asynchronous execution of computing arrays to overlap memory access latency.
1.19–1.61x speedup over state-of-the-art in-cache computing architectures with only 6.5 KB of additional storage overhead.
limitations: Speedup range of 1.19–1.61x is moderate; the paper does not discuss energy efficiency or compare against near-memory processing alternatives in the abstract.
primary_theme: Cacheline-granularity virtual in-cache computing with dynamic row allocation
